extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students/scholars of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, recognition, diction, chorus and episodes), with examples from Greek tragedy and epic. Emphasises unity, probability/necessity, and artistic modes of recognition/reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot — unity and causal construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must have a coherent structure (beginning, middle, end) in which incidents arise from the plot itself and follow by necessity or probability; the complication and the unravelling must be organically connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complication = beginning to the turning-point; Unravelling = change to the end. Avoid extraneous incidents that do not follow from the plot. The plot's events must not be due to random chance; both complication and unravelling should be derived from the plot's internal causes. Example: the Odyssey's episodic parts are largely episodes; in drama episodes should be short and relevant. Anti-pattern: converting an epic multiplicity of plots into a single tragedy (making a tragedy out of the whole Iliad) leads to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot — types of tragic action (reversal & recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots depend on reversal of situation (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis); other kinds are the pathetic (driven by passion), the ethical (driven by moral character), and the simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, combine reversal and recognition for greatest effect. The complex (with reversal and recognition) is the most powerful form of tragedy. Examples: reversals/recognitions in works by Sophocles and others. Anti-pattern: purely spectacular or episodic pieces where these elements are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of horrific/irreparable deeds — four modes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four ways a dreadful deed can occur in a plot: (1) done knowingly by those who know the persons, (2) done unwittingly with discovery afterwards, (3) one is about to act knowing the persons and then refrains, (4) one is about to act in ignorance and discovers before doing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these, the worst is (3): being about to act knowing and then not acting (shocking without tragic consequence). Better is (1) or (2), and the best is (4) — discovery before action that prevents the deed (e.g., Cresphontes Merope, Iphigenia). Examples: Medea (1), Oedipus (2/recognition outside drama), Antigone/Haemon episode (3 rare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina for internal resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deus ex Machina is permissible only for events external to the drama (antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge); it must not be used to resolve internal plot complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let irrational or externally imposed resolutions occur within the action (e.g., avoid deus ex machina to untangle the main plot). If something irrational cannot be excluded, place it outside the drama proper, as in Oedipus' irrational elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — moral goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Character should be good in the sense that speech or action manifests a morally purposeful aim; goodness is relative to the class (a woman or slave can be 'good' even if considered inferior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to give characters purposes that manifest moral intentionality. Avoid motiveless degradation (e.g., Menelaus in Orestes is an example of motiveless degradation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — propriety/appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must have traits appropriate to their kind: courage appropriate to men but generally inappropriate for women; certain cleverness may be inappropriate in some characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each trait is fitting to the character's social/psychological type. Anti-pattern: attributing manly valour as a general characteristic to a woman or other inappropriate mismatches (examples: inappropriateness in Odysseus' lament or Melanippe's speech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — likeness to life (probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must be true to life — actions and speech should follow by necessity or probability from the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should aim at what is necessary or probable; a person of a given character should speak or act in ways consistent with necessity or probability. Example: avoid having a character act in ways that contradict believable motivation unless the inconsistency is itself portrayed consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — consistency (even if inconsistent originally)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the model subject is inconsistent, the poet must represent that inconsistency consistently — 'consistently inconsistent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sudden, unjustified changes in a character's nature (e.g., Iphigenia at Aulis showing inconsistent behaviour across scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) — prefer natural, incident-derived recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is best when it arises naturally from the incidents themselves (a startling discovery made by natural means); other modes are less artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best: recognition that can be plausibly produced by the plot's events (e.g., Oedipus' discovery). Next best: recognition by reasoning. Lesser: memory-triggered recognition, turn of incident (Bath Scene), congenital or acquired tokens/signs. Least artistic: recognitions invented at will by the poet (artificial revelations) or formal proofs/tokens used expressly for proof. Examples: Odysseus scar (token, skillful), nurse/swineherd reporting differences; anti-pattern: Orestes speaking to reveal himself merely because poet wishes it rather than plot requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition — ranking of kinds (artistic value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of recognition are ranked: (least artistic) recognition by signs/tokens -> recognition by poet-invented revelation/voice -> memory-triggered recognition -> recognition by reasoning -> (best) recognition emerging from the incidents themselves, causing surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that dispense with artificial tokens and arise from incidents; avoid relying primarily on formal tokens or on manufactured verbal revelations that the plot does not require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial or deus-driven recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions that depend on token proofs or poet's fiat are less artistic and often unconvincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create recognition simply by having a character state facts the poet wants revealed; tokens used purely as proof are the least artistic form. Example negative: the 'voice of the shuttle' or Orestes declaring himself because the poet chooses to have him do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation / character portrayal — ennobling the type
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should imitate like a good portrait-painter: preserve the distinctive form of the original but produce a likeness that is true to life and yet more beautiful; make types better rather than degrade them needlessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray defects yet 'ennoble' the character (e.g., Achilles as portrayed by Agathon and Homer). Avoid gratuitous degradation or inconsistent depiction of moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity in plot & character
rubrics_metrics.description: Both complication and unravelling and the characters' actions must follow by necessary or probable sequence; the poet must work from what is necessary or probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use necessity/probability to link incidents; avoid having the unraveling occur through implausible means. Examples: avoid 'Deus ex Machina' or inexplicable contrivances; the discovery and resolutions must be rooted in the plot's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes — relevance, length and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes should be short in drama and directly relevant to the action; fill in episodes after sketching the general plan, ensuring they are pertinent and cohesive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch general outline first, then add episodes that are relevant. In drama the episodes must be concise (unlike epic); avoid long epic-like digressions. Examples: in the Iphigenia the sequence of events is tightly focused; anti-pattern: long expanded episodes that dilute the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus — integrated participant
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus should be regarded as an actor and an integral part of the whole, sharing in the action (not mere interludes as in later poets). The chorus should be of a size appropriate to unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make choral songs relevant to the subject; avoid the Agathon-style practice where choral songs are mere interludes unrelated to the drama. Chorus should help advance or reflect the action, not interrupt it arbitrarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Thought — rhetorical/psychological functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought includes proof/refutation and the excitation of feelings (pity, fear, anger). Diction involves the figures and structural elements of speech; both need mastery for producing effects by speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical devices and speech architecture (commands, prayers, narrative, threats, questions, answers) appropriately to prepare what speech must accomplish. Knowledge of rhetorical method is required; ensure speech produces the intended intellectual and emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative realism — visualize the scene and use appropriate gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene 'before his eyes' and work out appropriate gestures to avoid inconsistencies and to enhance realism (people who feel emotion act convincingly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thinking as a spectator helps spot mismatches (example: Carcinus/Amphiaraus oversight). Actors' gestures and emotional states must be convincing: agitation/aggression portrayed naturally. The poet needs either natural talent or an inspired strain (madness) to realize such convincing portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs/tokens in recognition — congenital vs acquired
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of recognition can be congenital (birthmarks, heraldic tokens) or acquired (scars, necklaces); these can be used more or less skilfully and rank lower artistically than incident-driven recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens permit less artistic recognition; they can be improved by skilful treatment (e.g., Odysseus' scar recognition by nurse vs swineherds). Use them with caution and prefer recognitions arising naturally from circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chance and rely on art for tragic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should not depend on mere chance to find tragic incidents; though some subjects come from 'happy chance' in myth, composition should rely on artful arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and adapt traditional materials with invention and skill without destroying essential legendary facts; show invention and skilful handling of traditional material (e.g., keeping core facts like Orestes slaying Clytemnestra while inventing plot variations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and scope — keep the dramatic form appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make an epic structure (multiplicity of large plots) into a drama; the parts must be of appropriate magnitude for the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic length requires different treatment; in drama, selecting portions and compressing is necessary. Anti-pattern: dramatizing an entire epic narrative (e.g., whole Iliad) leads to failure or poor stage results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional preparation — arousing pity, fear, anger
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must prepare the means by which speech and action will elicit pity, fear, anger and similar affects; these materials should follow from the argument and incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the parts of thought (proof/refutation, preparation of suffering etc.) to produce intended emotions. Some things should be shown without didactic explanation; others must be prepared by speech. Mastery of these techniques is required for effective tragic impact.
